blocks.heading: Key Concepts
blocks.html:
• Liver: largest internal organ — metabolic, synthetic, excretory, immune functions
  • Hepatocytes produce: albumin, clotting factors, bile, cholesterol
  • Kupffer cells: hepatic macrophages
  • Portal vein delivers nutrient-rich blood from GI tract
  • Bile: emulsifies fats, bilirubin excretion, stored in gallbladder
  • ALT (hepatocellular) and AST (mitochondrial) = liver injury markers

blocks.heading: Normal Values
blocks.html:
• ALT: 7-56 U/L
  • AST: 10-40 U/L
  • ALP: 44-147 U/L
  • Bilirubin total: 0.1-1.2 mg/dL
  • Albumin: 3.5-5.0 g/dL
  • PT/INR: 11-13.5s / 0.9-1.1
  • Ammonia: 15-45 mcg/dL

blocks.heading: What the Nurse Must Know
blocks.html:
• Hepatitis A: fecal-oral, acute, no chronic carrier state, vaccine available
  • Hepatitis B: blood/sexual/perinatal, can be chronic, vaccine available
  • Hepatitis C: blood-borne, high chronic rate, NO vaccine (but curable with DAAs)
  • Hepatitis D: requires HBV co-infection
  • Hepatitis E: fecal-oral, high mortality in pregnancy

blocks.heading: NORMAL FUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Liver metabolizes nutrients, detoxifies, synthesizes proteins
  • Normal bile flow and bilirubin excretion
  • Intact hepatocytes with normal enzyme levels
  • Normal clotting factor synthesis

blocks.heading: DYSFUNCTION
blocks.html:
• Hepatocellular injury: viral, alcoholic, drug-induced, autoimmune
  • Cholestasis: impaired bile flow → jaundice, pruritus
  • Cirrhosis: fibrosis replaces functional tissue → portal hypertension
  • Hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia accumulation → neurotoxicity
  • Liver failure: inability to perform essential functions

blocks.heading: ⚠ Risk Factors (Non-Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Genetic hemochromatosis, Wilson disease
  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
  • Autoimmune hepatitis (women 3-4x)

blocks.heading: 💡 Risk Factors (Modifiable)
blocks.html:
• Hepatitis B/C infection (chronic)
  • Alcohol abuse (most common cause of cirrhosis in Caribbean)
  • Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/NASH)
  • Medications: acetaminophen overdose, amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Aflatoxin exposure (contaminated grains — relevant in tropics)

blocks.heading: 🔥 Complications
blocks.html: Portal hypertension → esophageal varices, ascites, splenomegaly • Hepatic encephalopathy • Hepatorenal syndrome • Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) • Hepatocellular carcinoma • Coagulopathy
NRG Opposite: Liver damaged → synthetic and metabolic functions impaired → portal hypertension + encephalopathy + coagulopathy

1. Hepatocyte injury: virus, toxin, alcohol, autoimmune

2. Inflammation: immune-mediated hepatocellular damage

3. Fibrosis: collagen deposition replaces functional tissue

4. Cirrhosis: regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous septa

5. Portal hypertension: increased resistance in portal vein

6. Decompensation: ascites, varices, encephalopathy, HRS

blocks.heading: Key Detail
blocks.html: Cirrhosis is irreversible end-stage liver disease. Compensated cirrhosis: no complications. Decompensated: one or more of ascites, variceal hemorrhage, encephalopathy, jaundice. Child-Pugh and MELD scores predict prognosis and transplant priority.

blocks.heading: Clinical Result
blocks.html: Portal hypertension: increased pressure in portal vein → collateral circulation (varices), ascites (transudate), splenomegaly. Hepatic encephalopathy: ammonia and other neurotoxins accumulate due to impaired hepatic clearance and portosystemic shunting. Coagulopathy: decreased synthesis of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) and thrombocytopenia from splenic sequestration.
NRG Sequencing: Each step leads to the next — understand the cascade to predict S/S and management

blocks.heading: Early / Mild
blocks.html:
• Fatigue, weakness, anorexia
  • Mild RUQ discomfort
  • Nausea, occasional vomiting
  • Pruritus (cholestasis)
  • Dark urine, pale stools (biliary obstruction)

blocks.heading: Severe
blocks.html:
• Jaundice (scleral icterus first)
  • Ascites, peripheral edema
  • Confusion, asterixis (hepatic encephalopathy)
  • Easy bruising, prolonged bleeding
  • Gynecomastia, spider angiomas, palmar erythema
  • Fetor hepaticus (sweet musty breath)

blocks.heading: Variceal hemorrhage: hematemesis, melena, hypotension
blocks.html:
• Variceal hemorrhage: hematemesis, melena, hypotension
  • Severe hepatic encephalopathy: coma
  • Hepatorenal syndrome: oliguria, rising creatinine
  • SBP: fever, abdominal pain, rebound tenderness
  • THIS IS A MEDICAL EMERGENCY

blocks.heading: Diagnostic / Assessment Findings
blocks.html:
• LFTs: ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin
  • PT/INR: synthetic function (prolonged = impaired synthesis)
  • Albumin: synthetic function (low = chronic disease)
  • Ammonia: hepatic encephalopathy
  • CBC: thrombocytopenia (hypersplenism)
  • Abdominal ultrasound: liver texture, ascites, portal vein flow
  • HBV/HCV serology
  • Alpha-fetoprotein: HCC screening

blocks.heading: Link Patho to S/S
blocks.html:
Hepatocellular injury → Elevated ALT/AST, fatigue, anorexia

Cholestasis → Jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools

Portal hypertension → Ascites, varices, splenomegaly

Hepatic encephalopathy → Confusion, asterixis, elevated ammonia

Synthetic failure → Coagulopathy, hypoalbuminemia, edema

blocks.heading: Cardiovascular
blocks.html:
• BP (hypotension with hemorrhage)
  • HR, orthostatic vitals
  • Signs of bleeding (bruises, petechiae)
  • Capillary refill

blocks.heading: Respiratory
blocks.html:
• Respiratory rate (tachypnea with metabolic alkalosis)
  • SpO2
  • Lung sounds (hepatic hydrothorax)

blocks.heading: Neurological
blocks.html:
• Mental status (hepatic encephalopathy: grade 1-4)
  • Asterixis (flapping tremor)
  • Focal deficits (exclude other causes)

blocks.heading: Key Laboratory & Diagnostic Tests
rows: Elevated = hepatocellular injury; AST:ALT >2:1 suggests alcohol
Prolonged = decreased synthetic function — predicts severity
Elevated in hepatic encephalopathy but does NOT correlate with grade

blocks.heading: Priority Actions
blocks.html: Assess for hepatic encephalopathy (mental status, asterixis, constructional apraxia). Monitor for variceal bleed (hematemesis, melena). Daily weights and abdominal girth for ascites. STRICT I&O. Low-sodium diet (2 g/day). No alcohol, hepatotoxic drugs (especially acetaminophen >2 g/day).

blocks.heading: 💊 Pharmacology - Nursing Monitoring
rows: Traps ammonia in gut, promotes excretion
Goal: 2-3 soft stools/day; monitor for dehydration
Reduce portal pressure, prevent variceal bleed

blocks.heading: Variceal Bleed & Hepatic Encephalopathy Alert
blocks.html: Variceal bleed: EMERGENCY — octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus then 50 mcg/hr infusion, ceftriaxone (prevent SBP), emergency endoscopy with band ligation. Hepatic encephalopathy: lactulose goal is 2-3 soft stools/day. Rifaximin reduces recurrence. AVOID sedatives and opioids (worsen encephalopathy).

blocks.heading: Lifestyle & Patient Education
blocks.html:
• ABSOLUTE alcohol abstinence
  • Low-sodium diet (2 g/day) for ascites
  • Protein restriction NOT recommended (maintains muscle mass)
  • Small frequent meals
  • Vaccination: Hep A, Hep B, pneumococcal, influenza
🚨 Report Immediately: Hematemesis or melena | Confusion or decreased LOC | Temperature >38°C (SBP) | Oliguria <400 mL/day | Severe abdominal distension or pain

blocks.heading: Nursing Diagnosis
blocks.html: Excess fluid volume related to portal hypertension and hypoalbuminemia as evidenced by ascites, peripheral edema, and weight gain 4 kg

blocks.heading: Goal / Outcome
blocks.html: Patient will demonstrate stable fluid balance with no further weight gain and reduced abdominal girth within 72 hours.

blocks.heading: Interventions
blocks.html:
• Administer spironolactone + furosemide as prescribed
  • Daily weights and abdominal girth measurement
  • Low-sodium diet (2 g/day)
  • Fluid restriction if hyponatremic
  • Monitor electrolytes and renal function daily
  • Assess for SBP (fever, abdominal pain, tenderness)

blocks.heading: Rationale
blocks.html: Aldosterone antagonism (spironolactone) plus loop diuretic (furosemide) in a 100:40 ratio is the standard for ascites management. Daily measurements detect fluid shifts. Sodium restriction is the cornerstone of ascites management.

blocks.heading: Evaluation
blocks.html: Weight decreased 2.5 kg. Abdominal girth decreased 4 cm. No fever or abdominal pain. Electrolytes stable. Patient verbalizes sodium restriction.
NRG Care Plan Formula: Problem → Goal → Interventions → Rationale → Evaluation

What system is being tested?

Gastrointestinal — hepatic synthetic and metabolic function

What is the priority?

Lactulose for encephalopathy + variceal bleed prevention + ascites management

What is unsafe?

Sedatives/opioids in liver disease, high-dose acetaminophen, unmonitored diuretics

What restores function?

Lactulose clears ammonia; DAA cures HCV; alcohol abstinence prevents progression

blocks.heading: 💡 Key Memory Aids for RENR
blocks.html:
• PT/INR most important: Prolonged PT/INR = decreased synthetic function — most important prognostic LFT
  • Lactulose goal: 2-3 soft stools/day — traps ammonia in gut for excretion
  • Ammonia does NOT correlate: Ammonia level does NOT correlate with encephalopathy grade — clinical assessment does
  • Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir: Cures HCV in >95% after 12 weeks — pan-genotypic
  • Variceal bleed: Octreotide IV + ceftriaxone + emergency endoscopy — medical emergency
NRG System Focus Formula: Liver Disease → GI → Hepatocellular injury + portal hypertension → Ascites + encephalopathy + coagulopathy → Priority: Lactulose + variceal prevention + ascites management

question.stem: A patient with cirrhosis presents with confusion, asterixis, and lethargy. Laboratory results show ammonia 95 mcg/dL. The physician orders lactulose. The patient's family asks why the medication is needed when the ammonia level is 'not that high.' What is the nurse's best response?

options.html: Explain that the ammonia level confirms severe encephalopathy requiring immediate treatment
Teach that ammonia levels always correlate with the severity of hepatic encephalopathy symptoms
Explain that lactulose works by trapping ammonia in the gut for elimination, regardless of the exact level
Tell the family that the ammonia level is actually normal and the confusion is from something else

question.rationale: The ammonia level does NOT correlate with the clinical grade of hepatic encephalopathy — some patients have severe encephalopathy with mildly elevated ammonia, while others have high ammonia with minimal symptoms. The clinical assessment (confusion, asterixis, constructional apraxia) guides treatment, not the lab value. Lactulose works by acidifying the colonic contents, which converts ammonia (NH₃) to ammonium (NH₄⁺) that is trapped in the gut and excreted in stool. Option A incorrectly states that ammonia 'confirms' severity. Option B is factually wrong. Option D incorrectly dismisses the hepatic encephalopathy diagnosis.

why.html: Ammonia level does not confirm severity — clinical assessment does
Ammonia levels do NOT correlate with encephalopathy grade
The confusion and asterixis ARE hepatic encephalopathy — do not dismiss
